name: Shannon–Wiener Diversity Index Calculator
seoTitle: Shannon–Wiener Diversity Index Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: The Shannon–Wiener index measures how uncertain you would be, picking one individual at random, about which species it belongs to. Free shannon–wiener diversi
summary:
The Shannon–Wiener index measures how uncertain you would be, picking one individual at random, about which species it belongs to. It returns species richness, shannon index H′, pielou evenness J′ and maximum H′ for this richness, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It rises with both the number of species and the evenness of their abundances, which is why it is the default diversity measure in ecology. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Shannon–Wiener Diversity Index
sections.html:
H′ = −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ, where pᵢ = nᵢ ÷ N

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
nᵢindividuals of species iindividuals
pᵢthat species' share of all individuals0–1
H′Shannon–Wiener indexnats
J′Pielou evenness, H′ ÷ ln S0–1

sections.title: How do I use the Shannon–Wiener Diversity Index?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: species 1 count of 40 individuals, species 2 count of 25 individuals, species 3 count of 15 individuals, species 4 count of 10 individuals, species 5 count of 6 individuals.

Substituting them into the formula gives species richness of 5, shannon index h′ of 1.41, pielou evenness j′ of 0.8786, maximum h′ for this richness of 1.61.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
H′ below 1.0Low diversitydominated by one or two species
1.0 – 2.5Moderatetypical of many temperate communities
above 2.5High diversityeven, species-rich assemblages such as reefs or rainforest

  • H′ is in nats when the logarithm is natural; versions using log₂ or log₁₀ give different numbers, so always state the base.

  • The index is sample-size dependent — a bigger sample almost always raises it. Compare rarefied values, or fix the effort between sites.

  • Pielou evenness J′ = H′ / ln S divides out richness, so a community can be poor but very even and score a high J′.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Mixing log bases between the index and the evenness calculation.
  • Comparing H′ from quadrats of different size or counted by different people.
  • Entering zeros for unrecorded species, which does not change H′ but does change richness.

faq.q: What is a good Shannon index value?
faq.a: There is no universal threshold: values between 1.5 and 3.5 are common in nature, and the number is only meaningful next to another sample taken the same way.

faq.q: What is the difference between H′ and the Simpson index?
faq.a: Shannon weights rare species more heavily; Simpson is dominated by the commonest ones.

faq.q: What does the Shannon–Wiener Diversity Index actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns species richness, shannon index H′, pielou evenness J′ and maximum H′ for this richness. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
